main.title: Persona 4
main.summary: Persona 4, released outside Japan as Shin Megami Tensei: Persona 4, is a 2008 role-playing video game by Atlus.

cards.text: Atlus released Persona 4 for PlayStation 2 in Japan in July 2008, followed by North America in December and Europe and Australia in March 2009. The role-playing game follows a student spending a year in the rural town of Inaba. The expanded Persona 4 Golden later reached PlayStation Vita in 2012 and additional platforms in the following decade.

The game takes place in a fictional Japanese countryside in 2011 as a player-named protagonist moves into the town of Inaba from the city for a year. During his year-long stay, he becomes involved in investigating mysterious murders with a group of friends while harnessing the power to summon physical manifestations of their psyches known as a Persona. Much like Persona 3 before it, the game features role-playing and simulation elements: the protagonist progresses through a cycle of days, explores dungeons while encountering enemies, and can forge relationships that can improve their Personas' strength in battle.

The plot of Persona 4 was inspired by the work of mystery novelists owing to its murder mystery premise, primarily as a way of differentiating it from its predecessor. The rural setting was based on a town on the outskirts of Mount Fuji; it was intended to be a "'nowhere' place" and is the central setting to have players sympathize with the daily life of the characters. The developers added many in-game events to prevent the game from becoming stale. During localization, numerous alterations to Japanese cultural references were made to preserve the effect as much as possible.

The release of Persona 4 in Japan was accompanied by merchandise such as character costumes and accessories. The game's music was primarily composed by series composer Shoji Meguro, with vocals performed by Shihoko Hirata. The Western releases came with a soundtrack CD with selected music from the game. The game received critical acclaim, with praise given to its gameplay, story, emotional depth, characters, and music. Golden received higher praise for its addition of new content and visual upgrades over the original. The latter, in addition to its numerous console ports in the early 2020s, sold around 2.5 million copies worldwide.

In retrospect, Persona 4 is often considered to be one of the greatest video games ever made by several outlets. The game would see manga and light-novel adaptations, and an anime adaptation by AIC ASTA. The characters of Persona 4 have been featured in several spin-off games, including the fighting game Persona 4 Arena (2012), its sequel Persona 4 Arena Ultimax (2013), the rhythm game Persona 4: Dancing All Night (2015), and the Nintendo 3DS titles Persona Q: Shadow of the Labyrinth (2014) and Persona Q2: New Cinema Labyrinth (2018).

main.title: Street Fighter IV
main.summary: Street Fighter IV is a 2008 fighting game developed by Capcom and Dimps and published by Capcom.

cards.heading: The main series returns
cards.text: Capcom and Dimps developed Street Fighter IV for the Taito Type X2 arcade hardware in 2008. It was the first new main entry in eleven years, following Street Fighter III. Expanded PlayStation 3, Xbox 360 and Windows editions arrived in 2009.

cards.heading: Two-dimensional fighting with 3D characters
cards.text: Three-dimensional character models fight on a two-dimensional plane, preserving the series' familiar spatial rules. Street Fighter IV received strong reviews and continued through several expanded editions: Super Street Fighter IV in 2010, Arcade Edition in 2011 and Ultra Street Fighter IV in 2014. Together, its versions sold over nine million copies. Street Fighter V followed in 2016.

main.title: Siren: Blood Curse
main.subtitle: A village seen by strangers
main.summary: Siren: Blood Curse is Japan Studio's PlayStation 3 survival horror game, first released on 24 July 2008. An American television crew becomes caught in the events surrounding Hanuda, a remote Japanese village where the inhabitants have become deadly Shibito. The adventure reimagines the first Siren with a different cast and structure. Its twelve episodes move between connected characters, allowing the same crisis to be seen from several vulnerable positions. Surviving a short assignment may reveal information whose importance only becomes apparent when control passes to someone else.

cards.heading: A village seen by strangers
cards.text: Siren: Blood Curse is Japan Studio's PlayStation 3 survival horror game, first released on 24 July 2008. An American television crew becomes caught in the events surrounding Hanuda, a remote Japanese village where the inhabitants have become deadly Shibito. The adventure reimagines the first Siren with a different cast and structure. Its twelve episodes move between connected characters, allowing the same crisis to be seen from several vulnerable positions. Surviving a short assignment may reveal information whose importance only becomes apparent when control passes to someone else.

cards.heading: Look through the pursuer’s eyes
cards.text: Sightjacking lets a character see through another being's eyes. Watching a Shibito's route can reveal when a passage is clear or where a guard is looking, but it also divides attention between the observer and the person in danger. The player must translate that borrowed view back into a safe movement through the village. Hiding and avoiding an encounter often matter more than fighting. The ability turns an enemy into a source of information without removing the threat posed when that enemy finally finds the character.

cards.heading: Episodes that meet in the dark
cards.text: Each episode contains linked chapters, with missions and story sequences giving the journey a clearer forward order than the earlier games' navigation system. Changing protagonists also changes the means available to survive, preventing every situation from having the same answer. Director Keiichiro Toyama and writer Naoko Sato returned to the series, with Hitomi Shimizu composing the score. The release through PlayStation Store made the episodic structure part of its distribution as well as its storytelling. Reviewers generally welcomed this more accessible route into Siren's unsettling world.

main.title: Wario Land: Shake It!
main.subtitle: Wario follows the promise of endless money
main.summary: Wario Land: Shake It! is Good-Feel's Wii side-scrolling platformer sending Wario into the Shake Dimension in pursuit of a Bottomless Coin Sack. Known in Europe as The Shake Dimension, it presents the greedy adventurer through hand-drawn animation and broad physical comedy. Holding the Remote sideways retains a familiar platform-game arrangement, while shaking and tilting add actions suited to Wario's strength and impatience. Rescuing the inhabitants provides the journey's immediate task, but the promise of an inexhaustible fortune is what persuades its unlikely hero to become involved.

cards.heading: Wario follows the promise of endless money
cards.text: Wario Land: Shake It! is Good-Feel's Wii side-scrolling platformer sending Wario into the Shake Dimension in pursuit of a Bottomless Coin Sack. Known in Europe as The Shake Dimension, it presents the greedy adventurer through hand-drawn animation and broad physical comedy. Holding the Remote sideways retains a familiar platform-game arrangement, while shaking and tilting add actions suited to Wario's strength and impatience. Rescuing the inhabitants provides the journey's immediate task, but the promise of an inexhaustible fortune is what persuades its unlikely hero to become involved.

cards.heading: Shake something and see what falls out
cards.text: Wario can stun enemies, pick them up and shake them to release items. Coin bags respond to the same treatment, making the controller movement a direct expression of his enthusiasm for money. A forceful ground punch affects nearby enemies and mechanisms, while tilting helps aim thrown objects. Vehicle sections also use tilt controls. These additions build on the shoulder charge and heavy landing that already define Wario's movement, giving the motion controls specific jobs inside the platforming instead of replacing every familiar action with another gesture.

cards.heading: The journey back becomes a race
cards.text: Breaking the cage at the end of most stages frees a Merfle and starts a countdown. Wario then has to return to the entrance before time expires, using machines that launch him into a fast dash. Maintaining that speed can break obstacles and reach otherwise inaccessible treasure. The same landscape must therefore support a careful outward exploration and a much quicker return. Hidden valuables and optional objectives encourage another visit, rewarding players who learn how the route fits together and where Wario can keep his momentum through the escape.

main.title: Phantasy Star Portable
main.subtitle: A new partner investigates what remains of the invasion
main.summary: Phantasy Star Portable is Sonic Team and Alfa System's PSP action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 31 July 2008. Set after Phantasy Star Universe and its expansion, it follows a created character partnered with Vivienne, a newly built CAST android. Their investigation reveals that the threat of the SEED has not entirely disappeared. The story gives the repeated missions a personal companion, while character creation lets the player determine who enters them. Science-fiction weapons, fantasy enemies and developing equipment connect the portable adventure to the broader Phantasy Star setting.

cards.heading: A new partner investigates what remains of the invasion
cards.text: Phantasy Star Portable is Sonic Team and Alfa System's PSP action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 31 July 2008. Set after Phantasy Star Universe and its expansion, it follows a created character partnered with Vivienne, a newly built CAST android. Their investigation reveals that the threat of the SEED has not entirely disappeared. The story gives the repeated missions a personal companion, while character creation lets the player determine who enters them. Science-fiction weapons, fantasy enemies and developing equipment connect the portable adventure to the broader Phantasy Star setting.

cards.heading: Build a character before building the collection of equipment
cards.text: The player begins by choosing a race and class, then adjusts features ranging from facial appearance to clothing, body proportions and voice. Those choices establish an adventurer whose capabilities continue to develop through combat and equipment. Missions provide repeated opportunities to use the character's current tools and acquire something more useful for the next expedition. The appeal lies partly in that continuity: a short assignment can still contribute to a longer career. Returning to familiar action becomes worthwhile because the character and the available equipment are no longer quite the same as before.

cards.heading: The mission structure leaves room for nearby companions
cards.text: A single-player story sits alongside cooperative multiplayer for up to four people, allowing the portable format to support shared expeditions. Tatsuya Nagata directed the game, with music including work by Hideaki Kobayashi, Taihei Sato and Kenichi Tokoi. International releases followed in 2009, before the sequel advanced the setting by three years. Phantasy Star Portable's contribution was to make the series' cycle of missions, equipment and personal character growth available on PSP, with the possibility of carrying that developed adventurer into a session played alongside other people.

main.title: Rhythm Heaven
main.subtitle: A small gesture at the right moment
main.summary: Rhythm Heaven is Nintendo's DS collection of musical minigames, released as Rhythm Paradise in Europe. The handheld is held like a book, with the action on one side and the touchscreen ready for a stylus gesture on the other. Each scene gives a simple task a rhythmic rule: tap, hold, drag or flick when the sound calls for it. The situations are playful and often absurd, but the underlying challenge is consistent. Listen closely enough to make an ordinary movement become part of the music.

cards.text: Rhythm Heaven is Nintendo's DS collection of musical minigames, released as Rhythm Paradise in Europe. The handheld is held like a book, with the action on one side and the touchscreen ready for a stylus gesture on the other. Each scene gives a simple task a rhythmic rule: tap, hold, drag or flick when the sound calls for it. The situations are playful and often absurd, but the underlying challenge is consistent. Listen closely enough to make an ordinary movement become part of the music.

cards.heading: Learn the cue, then trust it
cards.text: Individual games introduce their actions through practice before asking for a complete performance. A visual event may help explain the pattern, but sound is the reliable guide to its timing. The stylus can flick a rod into a widget or follow another task whose rules fit a few repeated gestures. The restraint makes small changes in rhythm meaningful. Once the movement is understood, attention shifts from learning more buttons to recognising a pause, anticipating a return and resisting the temptation to act too early.

cards.heading: The remix remembers everything
cards.text: The fifty rhythm games are arranged into sets that combine several activities in a Remix. A single song can move between rules already learned, testing whether the player can recall an action when its sound returns. Strong performances award medals that unlock additional amusements and guitar lessons, while selected Perfect attempts demand an uninterrupted run. The structure gives repetition a clear purpose. A scene first completed with effort can later feel effortless, and the remix reveals that those separate little routines belong to one musical vocabulary.

main.title: Braid
main.subtitle: A mistake can become a tool
main.summary: Jonathan Blow's puzzle-platformer makes reversing time something to think with.

cards.heading: Rewinding changes the puzzle
cards.text: Braid lets the player rewind actions, but its puzzles give that power different rules and consequences. An apparent failure can expose a useful relationship between moving objects, timing and memory.

cards.heading: A smaller production finds an audience
cards.text: Released in 2008, Braid became a prominent example of smaller independent productions reaching players through digital distribution. Its puzzles develop variations on reversing time, giving each world a distinct use for the same central ability.

cards.heading: Time is a tool
cards.text: Braid is played by solving physical puzzles in a standard platform game environment. The player controls the protagonist Tim as he runs, jumps, and climbs across the game's levels. Tim jumps and stomps on enemies to defeat them, and can collect keys to unlock doors or operate levers to trigger platforms. A defining game element is the player's unlimited ability to reverse time and "rewind" actions, even after dying. The game is divided into six worlds, which are experienced sequentially and can be entered from different rooms of Tim's house; the player can return to any world previously visited to attempt to solve puzzles they missed.

cards.heading: Time and Forgiveness
cards.text: 2. Time and Forgiveness plays as an ordinary platform game, except that the player may rewind time to undo their actions. The section includes several challenges that would be unplayable or unfair in an ordinary platform game, but become feasible when the rewind mechanic is available.

cards.heading: Time and Mystery
cards.text: 3. Time and Mystery introduces objects surrounded by a green glow that are unaffected by time manipulation; for example, switches will remain flipped even if time is rewound to before the action occurred. Rewinding can thus be used to change the synchronization between objects that can and cannot be rewound, the basis of many puzzles in this section. This theme is also used in later worlds to denote objects unaffected by the player's time manipulation.

main.title: Ratchet & Clank Future: Quest for Booty
main.subtitle: A shorter voyage in search of Clank
main.summary: Ratchet & Clank Future: Quest for Booty is Insomniac Games' PlayStation 3 adventure, released on 21 August 2008. After Clank's disappearance in Tools of Destruction, Ratchet and Talwyn seek a way to contact the Zoni, following a lead connected to a legendary space pirate. The compact campaign places greater emphasis on exploration, puzzles and platforming than the surrounding games. Ratchet's wrench becomes more than a weapon, supplying practical ways to manipulate the island environments. The familiar hero enters a smaller story whose progress depends on handling the space around him as well as defeating its occupants.

After Clank's disappearance in Tools of Destruction, Ratchet and Talwyn seek a way to contact the Zoni, following a lead connected to a legendary space pirate. The compact campaign places greater emphasis on exploration, puzzles and platforming than the surrounding games. Ratchet's wrench becomes more than a weapon, supplying practical ways to manipulate the island environments. The familiar hero enters a smaller story whose progress depends on handling the space around him as well as defeating its occupants.

cards.heading: Use the wrench to move the obstacle
cards.text: The Omniwrench Millennium 12 can pick up objects and use a tether to alter parts of the environment. These interactions turn a blocked route into something to investigate rather than simply a place where another enemy wave must be cleared. Heliogrubs provide light in dark areas, adding another object whose handling changes what can be reached. Familiar weapons return from Tools of Destruction, but they share attention with those more deliberate tasks. The player reads the next room for a mechanism, movable object or source of light before deciding which tool should be used.

cards.heading: A bridge within the Future story
cards.text: David Bergeaud composed the music for a release positioned between Tools of Destruction and the later continuation of Ratchet's search. Its pirate setting gives the short journey a clear local character while keeping the larger mystery unresolved. PlayStation Network distribution allowed the game to work at a more compact scale than the usual console adventure. That scale suits its emphasis on puzzles and physical interaction. Quest for Booty uses an established character and set of abilities to explore another rhythm, allowing a brief island journey to carry the continuing series forward without pretending to be its final destination.

main.title: Inazuma Eleven
main.subtitle: A football team becomes a role-playing party
main.summary: Inazuma Eleven is Level-5's Nintendo DS football role-playing game about goalkeeper Mark Evans and the struggling team at Raimon Junior High. Building a capable squad and pursuing the Football Frontier competition turn a school sporting ambition into a larger adventure. Exploring, meeting potential recruits and developing the players take place between matches, giving the team a history beyond the result on the pitch. The combination makes football the shared purpose of a growing cast, with dramatic special techniques giving its sporting contests the energy of an animated adventure.

Building a capable squad and pursuing the Football Frontier competition turn a school sporting ambition into a larger adventure. Exploring, meeting potential recruits and developing the players take place between matches, giving the team a history beyond the result on the pitch. The combination makes football the shared purpose of a growing cast, with dramatic special techniques giving its sporting contests the energy of an animated adventure.

cards.heading: Recruitment changes the shape of the team
cards.text: The role-playing structure gives attention to who joins the squad and how the players develop. Exploring the surrounding places introduces people whose abilities may contribute to a stronger formation, while the continuing story gives Raimon's matches an immediate objective. Building the team becomes a process of discovering useful differences between its members. A new recruit has a place within a collective arrangement, and the next match provides an opportunity to see what that arrangement can do when the opposing side presents another challenge to overcome on the pitch.

cards.heading: The school competition opens a larger series
cards.text: The original adventure established the mixture of football, recruitment and character drama that continued through sequels and adaptations. Japan received the DS game in 2008, while Nintendo brought it to Europe in 2011. Its later Nintendo 3DS version extended access to the same first story rather than beginning another chapter. The opening team's modest situation remains important to the premise: success means helping a specific group develop enough to pursue its ambition, giving each new ability and each important match a place within a recognisable journey from an unpromising start.

main.title: Castle Crashers
main.summary: Castle Crashers is a beat 'em up video game developed and published by The Behemoth for the Xbox 360.

cards.text: Castle Crashers is a beat 'em up video game developed and published by The Behemoth for the Xbox 360. It was originally released on August 27, 2008 by Microsoft Game Studios via Xbox Live Arcade as part of the Xbox Live Summer of Arcade.  A PlayStation 3 version was released in North America on August 31, 2010, and November 3, 2010, in Europe via the PlayStation Network. A Microsoft Windows and OS X version, exclusive to Steam, was released on September 26, 2012. The game is set in a fictional medieval universe in which a dark wizard steals a mystical crystal and captures four princesses. Four knights are charged by the king to rescue the princesses, recover the crystal, and bring the wizard to justice. The game includes music created by members of Newgrounds.

On June 15, 2015, The Behemoth announced Castle Crashers Remastered for Xbox One, while the Steam version received it in the form of a free update. The remastered version features higher quality textures, higher frame-rate, performance improvements, and an additional mini-game. This version later released for the Nintendo Switch and PlayStation 4 on September 17, 2019. On August 6, 2025, the Painter Boss Paradise DLC was released for the Steam version of the game.
